title: Private data, no public doors
scenario: "The customer database and the secrets store must not have a public endpoint. Applications authenticate with Entra ID only — no SQL passwords anywhere." — CISO
mission: Deploy Key Vault and Azure SQL behind private endpoints with Entra-only authentication, and store the first secret out-of-band.
objectives: Explain private endpoints and their DNS
Configure Entra-only SQL with an admin group
Keep secret values out of Terraform state

prerequisites.notes: Your current public IP must be in operator_ip_ranges.

steps.title: Read the code
steps.detail: Find in 30-data: public network flags, the Entra admin, the private endpoints and their DNS zone groups.

steps.title: Store the banner secret
steps.detail: Create the portal-banner secret with az keyvault secret set (value never in Git or Terraform).

steps.title: Look at DNS
steps.detail: Resolve the Key Vault name from your machine and explain the CNAME chain.

criteria.text: Two private endpoints with IPs in 10.60.8.0/24
SQL server has public network access disabled
Secret portal-banner exists (name only — the value is never read)

expectedResult: Data services reachable only from the VNet, identities instead of passwords.

concepts.title: Private endpoints
concepts.body: A private endpoint puts a network interface with a private IP of YOUR VNet in front of a PaaS service (SQL, Key Vault). Traffic stays on the Microsoft backbone; you can then disable the public endpoint.

concepts.title: DNS makes it work
concepts.body: Clients keep using the normal name (`<name>.vault.azure.net`). Azure answers with a CNAME to `<name>.privatelink.vaultcore.azure.net`. Inside VNets linked to the private zone, that name resolves to the private IP; outside, to a public IP that is blocked. A *DNS zone group* on the endpoint registers the A record automatically.

concepts.title: Entra-only SQL and out-of-band secrets
concepts.body: With Entra-only authentication SQL has no password logins; an Entra group is the admin and applications use managed identities. Secret *values* are set with the CLI outside Terraform, so they never land in Terraform state.

example.title: following a CNAME chain
example.body: From your laptop, resolving any Azure service with a private endpoint shows the chain (public view):
example.code: Resolve-DnsName <name>.vault.azure.net | Select-Object Name, Type, NameHost, IPAddress

glossary.def: The Azure technology behind private endpoints.
Endpoint setting that writes its A record into the private DNS zone.
An Entra identity for an Azure resource, with no secret to manage.

recovery: ForbiddenByFirewall on Key Vault = network layer (your IP changed?), not RBAC. Separate network → identity → authorization.
dont: Do not put the secret value in azurerm_key_vault_secret
Do not enable SQL public access to "test quickly"
hints: Which Terraform attribute controls public network access on SQL and on Key Vault?
A private endpoint needs a private DNS zone group to register its A record.

interview.question: Draw how a private endpoint name resolves from inside and outside the VNet.
followUps: Why not manage secret values in Terraform?

debrief: Outside the VNet, <name>.vault.azure.net CNAMEs to privatelink.vaultcore.azure.net and resolves to a public IP that is firewalled. Inside, the linked private zone answers with the private endpoint IP. Secret values set out-of-band never land in state.
